messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: log likelihood? joint? posterior? reported in output
parts:
Andrew was suggesting that we add the log probability
to our output to support some * information criteria
calcs.

It looked like WAIC needed a log LIKELIHOOD, not
a log posterior or log joint. There's NOT a good
way to get at that in Stan, because Stan doesn't know
what the user is thinking of as data.

I could start thinking about how we can generate
code to calculate a log likelihood using the data
specification as the data (but this doesn't seem to
be what we want in the mixture indicator variable
case, as mixture indicators need to be specified as
parameters; on the other hand, we could sum out
the mixture indicator in this case in the program).

The problem is that for SAMPLING, a Stan model only
requires the log posterior up to a proportion. That's
the only thing that's going to be straightforward to
calculate and report.

For instance, the fully specified model

parameters { double(0,1) theta; }
model { theta ~ beta(1,1); }

and the underspecified model

parameters { double(0,1) theta; }
model { }

behave the same way with respect to sampling,
because beta_log(theta|1,1) = constant.

But there's no way for the second program to recover
the normalized log joint or log posterior, even though it'll
sample just fine.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log likelihood? joint? posterior? reported in output
parts:
Hi--I talked more with Aki today. What I learned:

1. I'm more sure than ever that we should be computing Waic. I don't think there's any need for us to compute DIC or any of the others.

2. Computing Waic is more effort than I thought, because we not only need the log likelihood, we also need the log likelihood for each data point. Which means that we need to save it as a vector for each iteration, or else go
back and compute it in post-processing at the end.

3. There are further complciations for models such as binomial where we want individual 0/1 data to be the "data points" for Waic, but the data might be coded as y-out-of-n.

I have thoughts on how best to do this, we can discuss further on Wed.

See you
A

parts: On 1/27/12 8:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> 2. Computing Waic is more effort than I thought, because we not only need the log likelihood, we also need the log likelihood for each data point. Which means that we need to save it as a vector for each iteration, or else go
> back and compute it in post-processing at the end.

Stan's not set up to require the user to even
express the likelihood in a way that's separable
from the joint probability calculation. This is
a similar problem to easily pulling out conditionals
for Gibbs.

> 3. There are further complciations for models such as binomial where we want individual 0/1 data to be the "data points" for Waic, but the data might be coded as y-out-of-n.
>
> I have thoughts on how best to do this, we can discuss further on Wed.

What about truly multivariate outcomes like
multivariate normal?

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: implementing Waic in Stan
parts: See below...
On Jan 29, 2012, at 4:06 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On 1/27/12 8:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>
>> 2. Computing Waic is more effort than I thought, because we not only need the log likelihood, we also need the log likelihood for each data point. Which means that we need to save it as a vector for each iteration, or else go
>> back and compute it in post-processing at the end.
>
> Stan's not set up to require the user to even
> express the likelihood in a way that's separable
> from the joint probability calculation. This is
> a similar problem to easily pulling out conditionals
> for Gibbs.

No, I'm not talking about anything as difficult as pulling out conditionals for Gibbs. What will be needed is (a) to flag the terms in the log-joint that correspond to the data model, and (b) separate the n different pieces corresponding to the n data points, thus saving a vector of contributions to the log-density. This will require further information to be passed to Stan. Alternatively, we could kluge it by just adding another line in Stan to compute the vector of contirbutions to the log-density. That would be ugly because it would require writing the "likelihood" part of the model twice, but for the models we've been considering (which have trivial Gaussian, binomial, etc. likelihoods and all the complexity is in the hierarchical prior), it would be easy enough to do.

>
>> 3. There are further complciations for models such as binomial where we want individual 0/1 data to be the "data points" for Waic, but the data might be coded as y-out-of-n.
>>
>> I have thoughts on how best to do this, we can discuss further on Wed.
>
> What about truly multivariate outcomes like
> multivariate normal?

This depends on the model, but I suppose the usual setting would be a (non-square) matrix of data, n by k, which would be considered as n observattions, each of which is a vector of length k. So for Waic we'd need to be saving n log-lik numbers for each iteration (or going back and computing n log-liks on the saved iterations, in a post-processing step).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] implementing Waic in Stan
parts:
It's easy enough to mark some of the variables
as what you and Jennifer called "modeled data".

data { int N; }
modeled data { double y[N]; }
parameters { double mu; double sigma; }
model {
for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}

The problem is that the likelihood terms for these aren't
as clear in Stan models as they are in BUGS (where
they're always on the left-hand side of a ~). For
instance, with the vectorized operations we were
considering earlier for efficiency, the model would
look like:

model { y ~ vectorized_normal(mu,sigma); }

and the function vectorized_normal(...) wouldn't even
have an individual term for the likelihood of an individual
outcome y[n] because it only computes the terms involving
sigma once.

This is different than having a vector y drawn
from a multivariate normal, which looks the same, but
apparently leads to only a single data point from
the WAIC perspective:

model { y ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma); }

In Stan, users can also write out the probability terms
themselves without using ~. And if we have things
like subroutines, it'll hide sampling details like
for the vectorized_normal example.

It'll probably be easier to talk about this at the
board on Wednesday.

- Bob
